terms.definition: The benchmark introduced in this paper, in which AI agents do synthesis, manipulation and interrogation tasks over professional-finance spreadsheets. The name is loosely inspired by building, understanding and editing financial spreadsheets.
The most capable, newest large language models from the leading AI developers at a given time.
The portion of a benchmark that is kept private rather than released, so models cannot be trained on it and results are not contaminated by leakage.
An AI model trained on large amounts of text that can read and generate language and, here, act as an agent using tools.
A language model used to grade other models' outputs against a rubric, here by inspecting the output workbook with tools.
The individual yes/no checks, each with a point weight, used to score an output. BLUEFIN has 3,225 of them.
A spreadsheet file, such as an Excel file, which can contain several sheets (tabs) of cells with values and formulas.
One sheet inside a spreadsheet workbook, such as a WACC tab or a DCF tab.
A valuation method that estimates a company's worth by forecasting its future cash flows and discounting them back to present value.
A BLUEFIN task family in which the agent builds a whole workbook from a natural-language prompt.
A BLUEFIN task family in which the agent modifies an existing workbook according to a prompt.
A BLUEFIN task family in which the agent answers a question about an existing workbook, graded against a known correct answer.
Described only loosely, so the agent must infer details and implicit expectations rather than follow explicit step-by-step instructions.
A unit equal to one hundredth of a percentage point; 1000 bps is 10 percentage points.
In lending, the percentage of an asset's value, such as inventory, that a lender will advance as a loan against it.
The starting workbook given to a task contributor, from which they build a modified or task-complete version.
An Anthropic language model that the authors used to draft candidate rubric criteria.
A rubric category checking that a formula implements the intended financial calculation, crediting any valid method.
A rubric category checking that a value is linked to its authoritative source tab rather than recomputed or hardcoded locally.
A rubric category checking that a key output matches a reference answer within a stated tolerance.
A rubric category that changes a driving input and checks that the dependent output recomputes to the correct new value.
A rubric category checking formatting and labelling conventions without changing the underlying numbers.
A rubric category of penalty checks for defects that degrade a model, such as error values or truncated text.
Typed in as a fixed number instead of being produced by a formula, so it does not update when inputs change.
The allowed margin of difference from a reference value, such as within ±2%, for a number to count as correct.
A spreadsheet error value shown when a formula refers to a cell that no longer exists or is invalid.
The software scaffold that gives an agent its tools, prompt and environment so it can attempt tasks and be run consistently.
The harness tool that recalculates all formulas in the workbook, so changed inputs propagate to outputs.
An open-source office suite; here its headless mode (no visible window) performs spreadsheet recalculation.
Formulas that depend on each other in a loop, as in debt schedules where interest depends on a balance that depends on interest; they need iterative calculation to settle.
A harness tool that runs sandboxed Python code to read or edit the workbook in bulk.
A Python library for reading and writing Excel workbooks.
A statistic measuring how well different raters agree on labels, corrected for chance; higher means more agreement.
A classification score that averages the F1 score (balance of precision and recall) across classes equally.
Runs where a model failed to produce a finished output; the paper scores these as zero.
The blended rate a company pays to finance itself with debt and equity, used as the discount rate in a DCF.
The total value of a company's operations, roughly what a buyer would pay for the business including its debt, net of cash.
The set of options that no other option beats on every measure at once, here both higher score and lower cost.
Describes an option that another option matches or beats on all measures, such as scoring at least as high at lower cost.
A revolving credit facility, a flexible loan that a company can draw on and repay repeatedly up to a limit.
The ongoing costs of running a business, such as salaries and rent.
The recorded sequences of actions and tool results an agent produces while working on a task.
